questions.q: What are the three parts of every QAOA circuit, in order?
options: State preparation (Hadamards), p alternating cost/mixer layers, measurement
Measurement, state preparation, classical optimization
Cost Hamiltonian construction, QUBO formulation, Ising conversion
Grover diffusion, amplitude amplification, phase estimation
questions.explain: QAOA always follows: Hadamards to create a uniform superposition, then p repetitions of alternating cost and mixer unitaries, then measurement of all qubits.

questions.q: How many tunable parameters does a depth-p QAOA circuit have?
options: p
2p
questions.explain: Each of the p layers contributes exactly two parameters -- gamma_k for that layer's cost unitary and beta_k for its mixer unitary -- giving 2p total tunable parameters.

questions.q: In the exact simulation of the single-edge Max-Cut circuit at gamma=pi/2, beta=pi/8, what measurement probability does the circuit assign to the uncut basis states |00> and |11>?
options: 0.5 each
0.25 each
0.0 each
1.0 each
questions.explain: Direct state-vector simulation shows the circuit assigns exactly 0 probability to |00> and |11> at these angles, placing 100% combined probability on the two cut states |01> and |10>, for an expected cost of exactly 1.0.

questions.q: Why does the mixer unitary U_B(beta), not the cost unitary U_C(gamma), do the work of redistributing probability between basis states?
options: Because U_C only applies phases to basis states (it doesn't change probabilities by itself), while U_B's Pauli-X-based rotations actually mix amplitudes across different bit values
Because U_C is never actually applied in a real QAOA circuit
Because U_B always sets every basis state's probability to be equal
Because the mixer unitary measures the qubits directly
questions.explain: U_C(gamma) is a diagonal phase operation -- it changes phases, not probabilities. It's the interference between those phases and U_B's amplitude-mixing (from Pauli-X rotations) that steers the final measured distribution toward good solutions.

questions.q: Why is QAOA called a 'variational' algorithm even though its circuit's gate structure is fixed in advance?
options: Because the circuit's 2p numerical parameters (the gammas and betas) are iteratively adjusted by a classical optimizer using measured expectation values as feedback, even though the gate layout itself doesn't change
Because the number of qubits changes every time the circuit runs
Because QAOA circuits randomly rearrange their own gates during execution
Because 'variational' simply means the circuit is simulated rather than run on real hardware
questions.explain: The gate structure (Hadamards, then p cost/mixer layers) never changes, but the parameters inside it are tuned by an outside classical optimizer in a hybrid loop -- the quantum hardware evaluates, the classical optimizer learns, which is the defining pattern this course revisits for VQE too.
